notes.summary: A cloze test is a short passage with five blanks. For each blank you choose the best of four options. Tier 1 usually has one cloze passage (five questions) and Tier 2 has more. Some blanks test vocabulary (which word fits the meaning, which word goes with its neighbour). Others test grammar: verb forms, connectors, prepositions, articles and pronouns. The secret is to read the whole passage first, decide what kind of word each blank needs, and only then look at the meaning.

concepts.title: Read the whole passage first
concepts.body:
Read the passage once from start to end without filling anything. Decide three things:
  1. Topic: what is it about?
  2. Tone: positive, critical, worried, neutral, a story?
  3. Time: is it in the past (a story) or present (general facts)?
Many blanks are decided by a sentence that comes after the blank. For example, The plan was ___. Within a year, it had doubled the village's income. The next sentence tells you the plan was a success.

concepts.title: Step 1: what kind of word does the blank need?
concepts.body:
Look at the words just before and after the blank.
Before the blankWord neededExample
a / an / the / adjectivenouna serious ___ (problem)
subject (he, the farmers)verbThe farmers ___ (grow) rice.
is / was / very / tooadjectiveShe was very ___ (kind).
tobase verb (V1), usuallyhow to ___ (use)
has / have / hadpast participle (V3)has ___ (grown)
between two clausesconnectorIt rained, ___ we stayed in.
Options that are the wrong part of speech can be crossed out at once.

concepts.title: Step 2: grammar checks
concepts.body:
• Subject-verb agreement: A single tap wastes (singular subject, -s verb); Taps waste.
  • Tense: keep the passage's time. A story in the past needs past verbs.
  • Active or passive: The school opened a new room (the school did it). A new room was opened (someone did it to the room).
  • After a relative pronoun, the verb agrees with the noun it refers to: drip irrigation, which delivers water.
  • Fixed patterns: how to + V1, look forward to + -ing, used to + V1, be used to + -ing.

concepts.title: Step 3: meaning and tone
concepts.body:
When two or three options pass the grammar check, choose by meaning.
  • Does the word fit the logic? A dripping tap can ___ thousands of litres → waste, not save.
  • Does it fit the tone? A passage praising a teacher needs positive words.
  • Is it too strong or too weak? The news was ___ received: warmly fits a happy passage, ecstatically is usually too much.

concepts.title: Connectors
concepts.body:
RelationConnectorsExample
Additionand, also, moreover, besides, in additionThe plan is cheap. Moreover, it is quick.
Contrastbut, yet, however, although, though, whereas, while, despiteAlthough he was tired, he kept working.
Resultso, therefore, thus, hence, as a result, consequentlyIt rained, so the match was cancelled.
Reasonbecause, since, as, due to, owing toHe was absent because he was ill.
Timewhen, while, after, before, until, as soon asTurn off the tap while you brush.
Conditionif, unless, provided that, in caseUnless you hurry, you will miss it.
Choiceor, either…or, neither…norNeither he nor I went.
Key pairs: not X but Y; not only X but also Y; both X and Y; hardly… when; no sooner… than.
while and during: while + clause (while we were eating), during + noun (during lunch).
although and despite: although + clause, despite + noun or -ing (despite the rain). Never despite of.

concepts.title: Collocations: words that go together
concepts.body:
Some words simply go with certain other words. Meaning alone cannot decide these.
UseNot
make a decision, make a mistake, make progress, make an effortdo a decision
do homework, do your duty, do business, do harmmake homework
take a risk, take care, take part, take a stepmake a risk
pay attention, pay a visit, pay a complimentgive attention (less natural)
heavy rain, strong tea, high temperature, deep sleepstrong rain, high tea (different meaning)
known for, famous for, rich in, proud of, afraid ofknown by (for a quality)
commit a crime, raise a question, reach a decisiondo a crime

concepts.title: Prepositions in passages
concepts.body:
• Time: at 6 o'clock, on Monday / 5 May, in May / 2024 / the morning; since 2015 (point), for ten years (period).
  • Place: at the station (point), in the room (inside), on the table (surface).
  • Fixed: interested in, good at, depend on, consist of, aware of, capable of, responsible for, similar to, different from, prefer X to Y, insist on, succeed in, accused of, charged with.

concepts.title: Articles, pronouns and quantifiers
concepts.body:
• a before a consonant sound (a university, a one-day trip); an before a vowel sound (an hour, an MLA).
  • the for something already mentioned or unique: a pump… the pump; the sun, the Ganga, the best.
  • Pronouns must agree with the noun they replace: The students… their books; The committee… its report (one body).
  • which for things, who for people, whose for possession.
  • much / little with uncountable nouns (much water, little time); many / few with countable plurals (many trees, few people).
  • a few = some (positive); few = hardly any (negative). Same for a little and little.

concepts.title: Final check
concepts.body: After filling all five blanks, read the whole passage once more with your answers in it. It should read smoothly, keep one tense and one tone, and not contradict itself. If one blank sounds odd, look at it again; the other four answers often give the clue.

varieties.name: Word that fits the meaning
varieties.how: All options are the same part of speech. Read the sentences around the blank and choose the word that fits the logic and tone of the passage.

example.q: A single dripping tap can ___ thousands of litres in a year. (save / waste / produce / hold)
steps: The passage is about careless use of water.
A dripping tap loses water; it does not save or produce it.
hold does not fit a dripping tap.

varieties.name: Word that goes with its neighbour
varieties.how: The options mean almost the same. Look at the word right next to the blank and pick the one that naturally goes with it.

example.q: He was ___ for his patience. (aware / known / proud / afraid)
steps: known for a quality is a fixed pair. aware of, proud of, afraid of take of.

varieties.name: Verb form and tense
varieties.how: Find the subject and the time of the passage. Check agreement, tense, active or passive, and any fixed pattern like to + V1.

example.q: Farmers use drip irrigation, which ___ water directly to the roots. (deliver / delivering / delivered / delivers)
steps: which refers to drip irrigation, a singular noun.
The passage is in the simple present.

varieties.name: Connector
varieties.how: Decide how the two ideas are related: addition, contrast, result, reason, time or condition. Then pick the connector of that kind.

example.q: ‘Learning,’ he said, ‘is not a race ___ a journey.’ (and / but / or / so)
steps: The pattern is not X but Y: one idea is rejected and the other is accepted.

varieties.name: Preposition
varieties.how: Check whether the word before the blank takes a fixed preposition (depend on, consist of). If not, decide by time or place rules.

example.q: The village has depended ___ the river for centuries. (in / on / at / with)

varieties.name: Article, pronoun or quantifier
varieties.how: Check whether the noun is countable, singular or already mentioned, and which noun a pronoun refers to.

example.q: There was ___ water left in the tank, so we had to be careful. (few / a few / little / many)
steps: water is uncountable, so few, a few, many are out.
had to be careful shows hardly any water was left, so little.

tips: Read the full passage once before filling any blank.
Decide the part of speech the blank needs; cross out options that do not fit.
Keep the passage's tense. A story in the past stays in the past.
For connectors, name the relation (contrast, result, reason) before reading the options.
Look at the sentence after the blank; it often settles the meaning.
Re-read the whole passage with all five answers filled in.
traps: An option that fits the single sentence but contradicts the passage's tone or the next sentence.
Near-synonyms where only one goes with the next word (make vs do, known for vs known by).
during before a clause: it should be while.
Verb forms that agree with the nearest noun instead of the real subject.
few vs a few and little vs a little: the positive and negative meanings are opposite.

passages.title: Saving Water
passages.text: Water is one of our most precious resources, yet we often (1)___ it carelessly. A single dripping tap can (2)___ thousands of litres in a year. Simple habits, such as turning off the tap (3)___ we brush our teeth, can make a real difference. Farmers, too, are learning to use drip irrigation, which (4)___ water directly to the roots of plants instead of flooding whole fields. If each of us takes small steps today, the growing problem of water (5)___ can be greatly reduced.

passages.title: The Old Teacher
passages.text: Mr. Iyer had taught in the village school for thirty years. He was (1)___ for his patience; no matter how many times a child got a sum wrong, he would explain it again with a smile. When the school (2)___ a new computer room, many expected the old teacher to retire. Instead, he spent his evenings learning how to type and how to (3)___ the internet. Within a few months he was helping the younger teachers prepare their lessons. His students noticed that he was never (4)___ to admit that he did not know something. ‘Learning,’ he often told them, ‘is not a race (5)___ a journey.’

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (1).
questions.solution: The word carelessly and the contrast word yet (after 'precious') require a neutral action done badly: use it carelessly. 'Save/protect/value carelessly' make no sense.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (2).
questions.solution: A dripping tap loses water, so it can waste thousands of litres.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (3).
questions.solution: A clause (we brush our teeth) follows, and the actions happen at the same time, so the conjunction while is needed. During is a preposition and needs a noun, not a clause.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (4).
questions.solution: which refers to drip irrigation (singular), and the passage is in the simple present, so delivers.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (5).
questions.solution: The passage is about wasting and saving water, and a 'growing problem' that saving reduces is a shortage: water scarcity. Abundance and surplus are not problems to be reduced.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (1).
questions.solution: The fixed phrase is known for a quality. The next clause describes his patience, so he was known for it.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (2).
questions.solution: The story is in the past and the school is the doer, so the active simple past opened is correct. 'was opened a new room' is ungrammatical.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (3).
questions.solution: how to is followed by the base form of the verb: how to type and how to use the internet.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (4).
questions.solution: The point is that admitting ignorance did not embarrass him: he was never ashamed to admit it. 'Never eager/happy/proud to admit' would give the opposite, negative picture, which does not fit the admiring tone.

questions.q: Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank (5).
questions.solution: The pattern not X but Y sets up a correction: learning is not a race but a journey.

flashcards.back: Read the whole passage once before filling any blank.
